newsitem.title: USA: Euro said unstoppable, but unemployment lurks.
newsitem.headline: Euro said unstoppable, but unemployment lurks.

text.p: The launch of European monetary union in 1999 is unstoppable, and Europe's partners in the Group of Seven are not even questioning whether it will go ahead on time, French officials said on Sunday.

Bank of France governor Jean-Claude Trichet said Europe had presented its plans for launching the new euro at talks between finance minsiters and central bank heads of the United States, Canada, Japan, Germany, France, Britain and Italy.
"The euro is there. No-one questioned the timetable for a second," he told reporters.
"The euro is recognized today. The timetable for the euro will be respected," French Finance Minsiter Jean Arthuis said.
"The launch of the euro in January 1999 has become an unstoppable reality for everyone," he added.
The G7 however, urged Europe to act to bring down its high unemployment, at record levels in France and Germany -- the two countries leading the drive to monetary union.

"In continental Europe, the principal task is to reduce persistently high unemployment, which has serious consequences for growth, public finances and for society as a whole," the G7 said in a statement.
It urged "structural reforms to reduce barriers to job creation, reduce the role of government in the economy and reform tax systems."
In the meantime, ministers from Germany, France and Italy all reaffirmed their determination to reduce budget deficits in preparation for the launch of the single currency.
German Finance Minister Theo Waigel said he stood by the German government's forecast that it would reduce its budget deficit to 2.9 percent of gross domestic product this year.
Speculation that Germany might overshoot a Maastricht treaty ceiling on budget deficits of three percent of GDP has been a major factor in fueling market speculation of a delay to monetary union.

Arthuis said he believed an early two-round parliamentary election in France on May 25 and June 1 would lift uncertainty and boost investment, creating the growth conditions to help it cut its deficit without any new budget cuts.

And Italian Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi said the G7 had expressed appreciation for Italy's efforts to ready itself for monetary union, though it was worried about the pace of its economic recovery.

"The G7 partners expressed appreciation for the curtailment of inflation, the solidity of the Italian economy, but also noted the slow rhythmn of its recovery compared to other European countries," Ciampi said, adding that the G7 said Italy might have to ease monetary policy.
"There has been a great appreciation for the very strong reduction of the budget deficit...There has been enormous progress. The judgement is positive," he said.

Trichet said European countries had also reassured their partners they would find a way to head off currency market speculation in the period between deciding in May 1998 which countries qualify to join monetary union and the launch of the euro in January 1999.
"It was a point which was very, very briefly raised, to say that we would find the means to avoid this completely," he said.
He declined to say what Europe would do to prevent markets speculating on what exchange rates will be used when countries joining monetary union fix their currencies irrevocably into the euro.
But officials have suggested Europe announce early how they plan to fix rates to prevent such speculation.
